To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

oscillatory coexistence can occur between competing predators feeding on a shared prey, that oscillatory coexistent states can provide transitions between two states of competitive exclusion, and that oscillatory behavior in a predator-prey model need not be a consequence of predator-prey interactions.
the coexistence of predators in a food chain is facilitated when one or both of the predators has an oscillatory behavior in its absence.
oscillatory predator coexistence can arise in a food chain with competing predators.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problem: How can the competitive exclusion principle fail?
the question whether the competitive exclusion principle is a universal law or not.
the question of how the oscillatory dynamics of one or more of a group of competing species may affect the dynamics of the group as a whole.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the principle of competitive exclusion is not valid for all parameter values in the model.
the competitive exclusion of one predator by the other is possible, but not necessary.
the competitive exclusion is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for a stable coexistence in the food chain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the competitive exclusion does not hold in the food chain model with oscillatory behavior.
the coexistence of the two predators is possible when the oscillatory predator is more efficient in utilizing the food than the nonoscillatory predator.
the coexistence of the two predators can be achieved by the oscillatory behavior of the predator.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oscillatory coexistence can occur in the presence of competing species, which is a new result in the field of population dynamics.
the coexistence of two competing species in the presence of a shared resource is possible even when the competitive exclusion principle holds for the species individually.
the competitive exclusion of species may be avoided in a system where the competing predators have oscillatory dynamics.
